_about: Hand-read clefs for EVERY staff on an orchestral page, top to bottom.
WHY THIS EXISTS. The sweep corpora are built from the staves the locator
fires on, so they measure precision and can say nothing about whether a
REJECTED staff was rejected rightly. That question needs a clef for every
staff, and until this file there were four such pages carrying ten C clefs
in total — too thin to tell a rejection from a loss, which is the only
distinction that matters when deciding where coverage is actually being
lost. `probe_cluster_too_big.py` is what reads it.
METHOD. `render_staff_heads.py` renders the head of every detected staff;
each was read by eye off the montage, and every C-clef call was then
re-read enlarged against numbered staff lines before being recorded
(`zoom` pass). Anything that could not be read confidently is null.
MATCHED TOP TO BOTTOM, not by system ordinal, because system grouping is
itself imperfect — beet9-p60 is really two systems of twelve and Phase 1
reports one of twenty-four. A page whose detected staff count no longer
matches `n_staves` is SKIPPED by the probe rather than mis-mapped.
'c-clef' means the glyph is certainly a C clef but the line it names could
not be read with confidence. It counts as a C clef and nothing more.
ORCHESTRAL SCORES ONLY, across four publishers: two Beethoven editions
from IMSLP, and Durand's Ravel and Debussy.
read_by: read off rendered staff-head crops by eye, 2026-08-31

pages.note: Phase 1 reports one system of 24; the labels repeat at ordinal 12, so it is really two systems of 12 that the connectivity grouping merged. Recorded top-to-bottom, which is why this file does not use system ordinals at all.

The choral finale, and the reason this page is here: six vocal staves in C clefs. Each is unmistakably a C clef; the LINE could not be read with confidence at this print's resolution, so they are recorded as the generic 'c-clef' rather than guessed at from the vocal convention. ord11 is the viola and its waist sits plainly on line 3.
A clean modern engraving, and the easiest reading in the file: both alto clefs put their waist exactly on line 3.

A heavily bled scan. Three staves are recorded as null rather than guessed: ordinals 9 and 10 show no clef in the crop at all, and ordinal 16 — which is where the viola should be — is a blob that cannot honestly be called a C clef. Omitting beats guessing.

The widest page in this file — 34 printed staves in one system, at the point where Ravel has the whole orchestra playing. It is here because the corpus needed a SECOND page carrying C clefs before anything measured on beet9-p120 alone could be trusted, and this one carries four in TWO kinds: the trombones read TENOR (waist on line 4) and the divided violas read ALTO (waist on line 3). Every other C clef in this file is an alto.

RECORDED AGAINST THE 31 STAVES THE PIPELINE SEES, not the 34 that are printed. Three of the printed staves are ONE-LINE percussion — Tambour, Cymbales, Grosse Caisse — carrying a percussion clef, which is neither a clef this file records nor something `transcribe` keeps: it drops all three and renumbers, so scoring 34 by ordinal would compare the harp against a cymbal. `detect_staves` alone DOES return them, each with a single line, which is why `render_staff_heads.py` shows 34.

⚠️ The viola at ordinal 26 here (staff_index 29) has a DETECTED window one staff space too high: its five lines land on the printed staff's top four plus empty space above, and the printed bottom line falls outside. Line-ink coverage over the full staff width is 0.41 for that top detected line against 0.99 for the rest — the signature `staff_detector._refit_misaligned_group` was built for, not caught here. The clef recorded is what the PRINT says, read against the printed lines. The pipeline reads that staff `mezzosoprano`, exactly one line below alto, which is what a window one space high does to a clef and is independent corroboration of both the misfit and the reading. Ordinals 1, 13 and 29 show a milder version of the same (coverage 0.41-0.55).
